## Formal {.unnumbered}
this is called eigen decomposition.
If there is a square matrix M, and determinant is not zero,
There is a diagonal matrix X

In linear algebra, the eigen-decomposition (or spectral decomposition) of a matrix is a factorization that breaks a square matrix down into its constituent eigenvalues and eigenvectors. This decomposition simplifies complex matrix powers and operations by transforming the matrix into a diagonal form.
Before defining the decomposition itself, linear algebra textbooks establish the rigorous definitions of eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

1. The Definitions of Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
An eigenvalue and its corresponding eigenvector represent a scalar-vector pair where a matrix transformation acts purely as a scaling or stretching operation.

Textbook Source
Book: Linear Algebra and Its Applications (5th Edition, 2016)
Authors: David C. Lay, Steven R. Lay, and Judi J. McDonald
Publisher: Pearson

The Formal Definition
In Chapter 5 ("Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors"), Section 5.1, the authors state:
Definition: "An eigenvector of an n×n matrix A is a nonzero vector x such that $Ax = \lambda x$ for some scalar λ. A scalar λ is called an eigenvalue of A if there is a nontrivial solution x of $Ax = \lambda x$; such an x is called an eigenvector corresponding to λ."


2. The Formal Definition of Eigen-Decomposition
The eigen-decomposition of a matrix unifies these individual pairs into a single matrix factorization. It relies on the concept of diagonalizability.

Textbook Source
Book: Linear Algebra (4th Edition, 2002)
Authors: Stephen H. Friedberg, Arnold J. Insel, and Lawrence E. Spence
Publisher: Pearson

The Formal Definition
In Chapter 5 ("Diagonalization"), Section 5.2, the matrix factorization known as the eigen-decomposition is formalized through the Diagonalization Theorem:

Theorem: "Let A be an n×n matrix. A is diagonalizable if and only if A has n linearly independent eigenvectors v1,v2,…,vn.

If A is diagonalizable, then

$A = P D P^{-1}$

where P is the n×n invertible matrix whose jth column is the eigenvector vj, and D is the n×n diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are the eigenvalues λ1,λ2,…,λn corresponding to v1,v2,…,vn respectively."

3. Structural Properties and Constraints
From these rigorous definitions, several essential mathematical properties emerge:
Matrix P Structure: The columns of the modal matrix P must be linearly independent. If an n×n matrix does not possess n linearly independent eigenvectors, it is called a defective matrix and cannot undergo a full eigen-decomposition.
Matrix D Structure: The diagonal matrix D holds the eigenvalues exactly in the same column order as their corresponding eigenvectors are placed in P.

$D = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & 0 & \dots & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_2 & \dots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \dots & \lambda_n \end{pmatrix}$

Geometric Transformation Interpretation: The decomposition asserts that applying the matrix A to a vector is equivalent to rotating the vector into an eigenspace coordinates system (P−1
 ), scaling along those axes (D), and rotating back back to standard coordinates (P).
